extracted.intended_audience: news editors, newsroom managers, journalists, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for newsroom decision-making about allegations of plagiarism and fabrication, describing factors to weigh and possible organizational responses. Uses historical cases to illustrate how severity, intent, position, pattern, and transparency shaped outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity and nature of the misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between types of wrongdoing (fabrication, plagiarism, minor attribution lapses) when deciding response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrication (inventing characters, quotes, phony datelines) historically leads to the harshest outcomes (e.g., Jayson Blair, Stephen Glass, Janet Cooke, Jack Kelley resigned or were fired). Plagiarism or improper attribution sometimes leads to suspension, correction or added attribution rather than termination (examples: Sari Horwitz suspended; Maureen Dowd's column was updated with a reference). Minor lapses (e.g., omitted attribution in a column) have in some cases resulted in corrections and notes rather than firing (Denver Post's Woody Paige).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope, scale, and pattern of the misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the incident is isolated or part of a wider pattern or multiple fabricated/plagiarized pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated or wide-ranging fabrication (Stephen Glass fabricated >25 stories; Jayson Blair used multiple fabrications and phony datelines; Jack Kelley fabricated parts of at least eight major stories) triggered full investigations and more severe sanctions than single, limited incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position, seniority, and reputation of the journalist
rubrics_metrics.description: Take into account the reporter's job status (staff, columnist, freelancer), years at the organization, and professional reputation or awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longtime staffers and award-winning journalists may receive different handling: Sari Horwitz (28 years, Pulitzer winner) was suspended and her work reviewed; Maureen Dowd (columnist) was not fired but her column was updated. Conversely, some longtime employees have been fired depending on circumstances (examples vary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of intent versus negligence or sloppy error
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the act was malicious/planned or a negligent/sloppy mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions of negligence or forgetfulness (e.g., Will Selva said he 'forgot' to rewrite cut-and-paste material) have in some cases led to suspension and apology, while clear, deliberate fabrication tends to result in termination or resignation. Statements by the journalist about intent are often cited by editors when explaining actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission, apology, and cooperation by the journalist
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the journalist acknowledges the error, apologizes, and cooperates with the investigation influences outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public apologies and admissions are common (several cited examples include apologies). Cooperation can temper responses but does not guarantee retention if the misconduct is severe (e.g., some who apologized were still suspended or dismissed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and documentation (review and investigation of prior work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct editorial reviews or internal investigations of the reporter's past work to determine extent and pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors often review other stories after an incident (e.g., editors reviewed dozens of Horwitz's stories and found none other plagiarized; USA Today conducted an internal investigation after Jack Kelley). Scope of review can affect the final sanction and any further public reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of fabrication or plagiarism (what was fabricated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different forms of fabrication (fabricated characters, fake quotes, phony datelines) and different plagiarism modes (lifting prose, unattributed paraphrase) carry different moral and practical weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invented characters or sources and falsified facts or datelines are described as especially egregious (Janet Cooke's fabricated 8-year-old; Patricia Smith made up characters), often leading to resignation/stripping of awards; lifted passages from other publications may be handled with corrections and attribution if limited, but extensive copying can lead to suspension or dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment/contractual status (staff vs freelancer vs contributor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the journalist's contractual relationship with the outlet when determining remedial steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freelancers may be quickly cut off from assignments (e.g., Village Voice freelancer Rob Sgobbo was told he could no longer freelance there and had relationships terminated elsewhere). Staffers may face suspension, resignation, or firing depending on internal policies and the severity of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational response options and proportionality of sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations may choose among corrections, added attributions, suspensions, terminations, resignations, rescinding awards, public apologies, or systemic changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples across cases: running a correction and adding an attribution (Denver Post's Woody Paige); suspending a reporter (Sari Horwitz, ESPN's Will Selva); firing or forced resignation for major fabrications (Jayson Blair, Stephen Glass, Janet Cooke); rescinding awards (Patricia Smith's ASNE award rescinded; Pulitzer revoked for Janet Cooke). Newsrooms weigh proportionality based on other factors (severity, pattern, intent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and public corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how transparently to inform readers (apologies, updated pieces, front‑page coverage of the scandal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some organizations published apologies and updates (The Post ran an apology for Horwitz; The Times ran a front‑page story on Blair). Transparency about actions taken and corrections issued is frequently used to restore trust and to signal seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on reader trust and institutional credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how the incident affects the outlet's credibility and the perceived promise of accuracy and honesty to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors cite the centrality of 'accuracy and honesty in reporting' when explaining sanctions (quote from Sun‑Times editor). Serious breaches that undermine trust often prompt stronger, public remedies and systemic reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for awards, recognition, and legacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to rescind earlier honors or awards connected to the work in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations or professional bodies may rescind awards when fabrication is found (ASNE rescinded Patricia Smith's award; Janet Cooke was stripped of a Pulitzer), which signals reputational consequences beyond employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-incident institutional reforms and safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Use incidents to evaluate and implement newsroom policy changes to prevent recurrence (e.g., better resume/source checks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After major scandals, newsrooms have instituted reforms (The Post devised a system for checking reporters' resumes and asked editors to be more deliberate about checking authenticity of characters and sources). Such systemic responses are part of remediation and prevention.
